newsitem.title: UK: Coffee market watches Zaire, no panic yet.
newsitem.headline: Coffee market watches Zaire, no panic yet.

text.p: Coffee traders kept a close eye on the crisis in Zaire following escalated fighting in the eastern part of the country where most of its crop is grown.
With the main Zairean crop is not due until December, traders said there was no cause for panic yet. But they said supplies could be threatened if chaos persisted.
"At this stage, no one is sure whether the situation in Zaire is really going to affect the whole of Zaire itself," said Lawrence Eagles, the head of research at UK brokerage GNI Ltd.

"So..I don't think anyone is looking at it any closer than that," he told Reuters. Zaire and its neighbouring Rwanda moved closer to war on Wednesday after two days of trading artillery fire on their border and a Rwandan sorties into eastern Zaire.
The crisis in its Eastern borderlands is seen as potentially the most far-reaching in Zaire's 36-year history as an independent state.
Rivalry between ethnic Hutus and Tutsis, which resulted in nearly one million dead in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, has spilled into Zaire, home to 1.1 million Rwandan refugees.
Fighting inside Zaire pits Zairean troops against Tutsi rebels apparently receiving support from Tutsi-led Rwanda.
Rwanda is also a coffee producer, along with neighbouring Burundi and Uganda, the latter being Africa's largest.

Eagles said: "This is one that clearly has to be taken very seriously but until we are in a situation where there is a major threat to supplies, the market is unlikely to react to it." A Swiss-based trader said the muted market reaction was also due to the fact that the main crop from the Central Africa state is not due until December.

"I think the volumes that are moving out now are not great anyway because it is slightly off season. So I don't think there's any specific immediate-term concern...there's a much greater longer-term concern." The eastern Zairean towns of Goma and Beni are two major grading centres for Zairean coffee.
"With the roads closed around Goma, you can't get out of Goma now. So the grading office is not functioning," he said.
At present, there are an estimated 727,000 refugees in the Goma area alone.
Zaire exports almost all of its coffee production.
Traders pegged Zaire exports at just above 20,000 tonnes in 1995/96 (Oct-Sept) against 29,000 in 1994/95. The year-ago exports included some 4,000 tonnes brought acrosss Rwanda.
Zaire's robusta crop has been suffering from a disease named tracheomycosis. The 1995/96 crop be around 15,000 tonnes, down from 19,000 in 1994/95 and could be lower still in 1996/97.
Zaire HTCM coffee, the origin benchmark, hovers at $50 under London on a CIF Europe basis, the same as the month-ago level. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 4985
